text: Will this flight leave more than 15 minutes late, or be cancelled? Predicted for every scheduled flight, 2 hours before its scheduled departure.

The share of all late-or-cancelled flights we reach when we warn the riskiest 1 flight in 5 (recall), with precision next to it. A missed late flight can strand a client or break a connection; a needless warning costs one message.

Two hours before each departure, warn the flight if its risk is above the cut-off set from the risk scores of the previous 7 days (the score of the riskiest 20% of those flights; it needs no outcomes and no future flights). Run like this from the 8th day of October to the end of December, it warned 20% of the flights and reached 40% of the late or cancelled ones, 28% of the warnings being right. If each hour's flights were ranked only among themselves (which already needs the scores of flights up to an hour ahead), the reach would fall to 34%; ranking the whole quarter at once (risk above 0.31), which no live system can do, reaches 40%. Chosen by capacity, assuming the agency can warn about 1 flight in 5 (to be confirmed), not by a fixed probability, because the scores ran high in the calm months (22% predicted against 14% real).

Warn those clients and check their connections. The list is the same for every destination; the advice differs by type: steady regional routes, a short heads-up and a backup for tight connections; afternoon build-up routes, offer a morning flight or a longer connection; thin routes, offer a flexible ticket and rebook early.

On the held-out months (October to December): 20,894 of 104,469 flights are warned (1 in 5). 28% of them are really late or cancelled (against 14% of all flights) and together they hold 40% of all late or cancelled flights. Picking 20,894 flights at random would reach 20%: the model reaches 2.0 times more. The dumb answer "nobody is late" warns nobody and reaches 0%.

A neural network (two small hidden layers) on 18 columns known 2 hours before: hour, weekday, airline, airport, destination type, distance, airport crowding, plane age and seats, the weather 2 hours earlier, and the delay of the same plane's earlier flight. Trained on the flights of January to September 2023.

PR-AUC 0.29 on October-December, against 0.14 for the dumb answer and 0.18 for a simple hour-of-day rule. The other two models, logistic regression (0.28) and gradient boosting (0.30), score about the same.

It reaches only 7% of the late flights in the Morning (before noon) band, but 70% in the Evening (6 pm on) band. By airline the reach goes from 19% (American Airlines) to 63% (JetBlue Airways). Risk scores run too high in calm months, so use the ranking, not the percentage.

Every week, once it is over: rank that week's flights by risk, warn the riskiest fifth and measure how many of the late or cancelled flights they hold (the weekly reach). The line comes from the July to September validation weeks (median weekly reach 37%; the line is 80% of it, 30%), not from the held-out weeks. Retrain when the weekly reach falls below 30% for two weeks in a row. In October-December the weekly reach was between 37% and 46%, and the rule would not have fired.
Before calling a client, a person looks at the plane's earlier flights and the weather, and handles clients on tight connections first. Nothing is cancelled or rebooked automatically.

When the same plane's earlier flight left more than 15 minutes late, 61% of the next flights are late or cancelled, against 25% when it left on time. This is already known two hours before departure for the 29% of flights whose plane's earlier flight had left at least 2 hours before.
How many minutes late will this flight leave? Predicted for every flight that leaves, 2 hours before its scheduled departure. (Cancelled flights are covered by card 1.)

The average error in minutes (MAE), with the median error next to it. Clients are told a number of minutes, so the error is read in minutes. A few flights of 5 to 30 hours weigh heavily in the average, which is why the median is shown too.

Check the connections of the 5% of flights with the highest predicted delay (predicted delay above 14 minutes in October-December). Chosen by capacity, assuming the agency can check 1 flight in 20 (to be confirmed). A "long" delay means 45 minutes or more.
For flagged flights: tell the client to expect a long delay, check the connection, and prepare a backup flight. Do not change the booking until a person has confirmed.

On the held-out months: 5,212 of 104,245 flights are flagged (1 in 20). 21% of them really leave 45 minutes or more late, against 6% of all flights (3.4 times more), and they hold 17% of all long delays (picking at random would reach 5%). On average the prediction is 0.14 minutes closer than the dumb answer (13.12 against 13.27 minutes).

Gradient boosting (many small decision trees, trained to minimise the absolute error) on the same 18 columns known 2 hours before, trained on January to September 2023. It predicts the usual delay of flights like this one.
Average error 13.12 minutes against 13.27 for the dumb answer (every flight leaves 2 minutes early); median error 4.5 against 5.0 minutes. A straight-line model (ridge) is at 13.46 minutes.

The gain in average error is small (0.14 minutes) and it does not come from a few extreme delays: the usual flight leaves close to schedule, so the usual-delay guess is already near, and without the 1% most delayed flights the gain is smaller still (0.04 minutes; the model's average error is 10.6 minutes). Errors differ by airline, from 7 minutes (Republic Airline) to 21 minutes (JetBlue Airways). Predicting the usual delay means it flags risk, not certainty.

Every week, comparing the model's average error with the dumb answer's. In the held-out weeks the model beat the dumb answer in 9 of 13 full weeks, and the rule below would have fired once: the gain is fragile. Retrain, or drop the model, when it is no better than the dumb answer for two weeks in a row.
A person confirms the plane's earlier delay and the airline's own status before telling a client to expect a long delay. Clients on tight connections come first.

Delay is a matter of risk, not certainty. In the tenth of flights with the highest predicted delay, one flight in ten leaves more than 74 minutes late, against 0 minutes in the lowest tenth, even though the usual flight in both leaves close to schedule.
